slmarket.seoTitle: SLMarket: a Live POS/ERP and a Marketplace, Built Solo
slmarket.seoDescription: How Arshed Ahmed built SLMarket alone: SLMarket Flow, a real-time Laravel POS/ERP that is live with real users, and a Next.js marketplace in development.
slmarket.outcome: Designed, built and shipped Flow alone; it runs live for real users.

case.problem: Shops in Sri Lanka needed one simple system for the shop floor: taking sales, tracking stock and keeping records, without stitching separate tools together. Buyers and sellers also needed one place to trade online, in the language they are most comfortable with.
context: SLMarket is two products. SLMarket Flow is the back office: a real-time POS with ERP features that shop staff use while they sell. It is live with real users. The marketplace at slmarket.lk is the storefront for buyers, and it is in development.
I own both end to end: product scope, data model, frontend, backend, tests, CI/CD and hosting.
case.architecture: Two independent applications. Flow is Laravel, Vue.js and Inertia.js on MySQL, deployed on cPanel. The marketplace is Next.js and TypeScript on PostgreSQL through Prisma, with Redis for caching and Cloudinary for media, deployed on Vercel. Both release through GitHub Actions.

decisions.title: Two stacks, one job each
decisions.why: Flow is a signed-in back-office tool, so Laravel with Inertia.js makes forms and CRUD screens fast to build. The marketplace is public and search-sensitive, so it is a Next.js app on Vercel.
decisions.tradeoff: Two codebases and two deploy targets for one engineer, in exchange for the right tool for each audience.

decisions.title: Relational data, cached reads
decisions.why: Listings, sellers and orders are relational, so PostgreSQL with Prisma keeps types aligned from the schema to the UI. Redis caches the read-heavy paths.
decisions.tradeoff: A cache means invalidation rules to get right whenever a listing or price changes.

decisions.title: Tests in CI before every release
decisions.why: As the only engineer, unit and integration tests running in GitHub Actions act as my reviewer before code reaches the shop floor.
decisions.tradeoff: Slower early iterations, in exchange for fewer regressions once real users depend on Flow.

challenges: Running a live POS alone: every feature, fix and deploy goes through one person, so automation carries the review load.
Role-based access and end-to-end order flows that hold up for owners, staff and sellers with different permissions.
improve: Add end-to-end browser tests on the POS sale and checkout flows.
Publish usage numbers from Flow once I can share them.

case.problem: To run as a SaaS, the platform needed reliable billing: one-time payments, subscriptions, plan changes with fair proration, and refunds. The team also needed to see payments as they happened, without digging through the Stripe dashboard.
context: The platform guides businesses on grants and funding through several AI chatbots. I worked across the Express.js backend and the Next.js frontend and owned billing from checkout to refunds.
Screens from this project are company work, so this page uses a redrawn schematic instead of real screenshots.
case.architecture: The Next.js frontend talks to an Express.js API that holds the payment and business logic. The API calls the AI chatbot workflows, creates and updates Stripe objects, and receives Stripe webhooks that keep payment records in sync.

decisions.title: Webhooks as the source of truth
decisions.why: Subscription and payment state is updated from Stripe webhook events, never from what the browser reports.
decisions.tradeoff: Handlers must cope with events that arrive late, twice or out of order.

decisions.title: Stripe's proration instead of custom maths
decisions.why: Plan changes use Stripe's automated proration, so charges stay correct without manual adjustments.
decisions.tradeoff: Billing rules follow Stripe's model, so unusual pricing has to fit its API.

decisions.title: Tests around money
decisions.why: Jest unit and integration tests cover the payment and API logic, where a regression costs real money.
decisions.tradeoff: Mocked Stripe responses can drift from the real API over time.

challenges: Keeping one payments flow for one-time charges, subscriptions and refunds instead of three separate paths.
Giving the team live payment visibility without handing everyone access to the Stripe dashboard.
improve: Add an audit log of every webhook event and the state change it caused.
Run contract tests against Stripe's test mode in CI to catch API drift.

case.problem: Job seekers often send CVs that applicant tracking systems parse badly, and they rarely get to practise interviews with useful feedback.
context: The platform helps candidates build an ATS-friendly CV tailored to a job description, then rehearse out loud in a voice mock interview.
case.architecture: A Next.js and TypeScript app handles the UI and server logic. CV generation, parsing and job-description matching call a Groq-hosted LLM. In the mock interview, Whisper turns spoken answers into text and the LLM writes feedback. Data lives in PostgreSQL through Prisma.

decisions.title: Groq for response time
decisions.why: A fast-inference LLM host makes CV suggestions and interview feedback feel immediate.
decisions.tradeoff: A narrower choice of models than the largest providers offer.

decisions.title: Speak, don't type
decisions.why: Whisper speech-to-text lets candidates answer out loud, as they would in a real interview.
decisions.tradeoff: Transcription adds a step, and time, to every answer.

decisions.title: Match before rewriting
decisions.why: The CV is compared against the target job description before any changes are generated.
decisions.tradeoff: An extra model call per tailoring request.

challenges: Keeping the voice round trip short enough to feel like a conversation.
Producing CV layouts that applicant tracking systems parse reliably.
improve: Stream feedback as it is generated instead of waiting for the full answer.
Build a small evaluation set to measure feedback quality between prompt changes.

case.problem: Customers already use WhatsApp every day, but answering every message by hand does not scale. The goal was to automate those conversations so people get answers without waiting for a person.
context: I built and deployed the bot at Softsora. Conversations from this project are company data, so this page uses a redrawn schematic instead of real screenshots.
case.architecture: Customers message a WhatsApp number connected through Twilio. Twilio forwards each message to a Python webhook service, which uses an LLM API to understand it and write a reply, then sends the reply back through Twilio.

decisions.title: Meet customers in WhatsApp
decisions.why: Twilio's WhatsApp API puts the bot in an app customers already have, with nothing new to install.
decisions.tradeoff: Per-message costs and WhatsApp's messaging rules shape what the bot can send and when.

decisions.title: A separate Python service
decisions.why: A small webhook service keeps the business logic apart from the messaging channel.
decisions.tradeoff: One more service to deploy and monitor.

decisions.title: Language model instead of menu trees
decisions.why: An LLM understands free-text messages, so customers don't have to follow rigid numbered menus.
decisions.tradeoff: Replies are less predictable than a fixed menu, so prompts need guardrails.

challenges: Answering within the messaging webhook's time limits while waiting on a language model.
Keeping replies on-topic for free-text messages that do not follow a script.
improve: Add a clean hand-off to a human agent for conversations the bot cannot resolve.
Log intents and outcomes so the team can see which questions the bot handles well.
